title: Integrative modeling identifies genetic ancestry-associated molecular correlates in human cancer
author: Robertson, Yau, et al.
materials: TCGA normalized mature strand miRNA RPM data

steps.title: Download ancestry assignment data
steps.instruction: Download raw ancestry calls and admixture estimates (Table S1, Carrot‑Zhang et al., 2020) from the GDC publication page (https://gdc.cancer.gov/node/1248). The file includes patient classification into EUR, EAS, AFR, Native/Latin American, and (South) Asian, as well as admixed individuals and their admixture levels.

steps.title: Compile cancer subtype tables
steps.instruction: Download Table S1 from Sanchez‑Vega et al., 2018 and the bladder cancer mRNA subtype table (Table S1, Robertson et al., 2018, column “mRNA_cluster”). Consolidate both sources into a single cancer‑type‑and‑subtype annotation table.

steps.title: Retrieve clinical age and gender data
steps.instruction: Download the “clinical with follow up” file from the Pan‑Cancer Atlas (https://gdc.cancer.gov/about-data/publications/pancanatlas) and extract the fields “age_at_initial_pathologic_diagnosis” (age) and gender for each sample.

steps.title: Obtain sample quality whitelist
steps.instruction: Download the sample quality whitelist from the Genomic Data Commons as listed in the key resources table.

steps.title: Download significantly mutated gene lists
steps.instruction: From the MC3 mutation call file (key resources), download the significantly mutated gene (SMG) lists for each cancer type generated by MutSig2 (Bailey et al., 2018). Merge all SMG lists to obtain a pan‑cancer set of significantly mutated genes.

steps.title: Create mutation frequency file
steps.instruction: For each SMG, count the number of samples that have at least one SNV or small indel (using the MC3 mutation call file) **or** a focal copy‑number amplification (using the pan‑cancer GISTIC copy‑number calls, defined as log2 copy‑number ratio > 1). Record these counts in a mutation‑frequency table.

steps.title: Exclude admixed samples and low‑frequency genes
steps.instruction: Remove samples with ancestry admixture between 20 % and 80 % non‑EUR (i.e., 20 % < non‑EUR ancestry < 80 %). Also remove any gene that has fewer than 30 altered samples in the AFR group. Two three‑way admixed individuals ( > 20 % ancestry in > 2 groups) are retained and will be analyzed separately later.

steps.title: Merge data with ancestry, clinical, subtype
steps.instruction: Combine the mutation‑frequency table with the TCGA ancestry assignments, the clinical age/gender file, and the cancer‑type/subtype annotation table.

steps.title: Encode variables and run logistic regression
steps.instruction: Code EUR ancestry as 0 and AFR ancestry as 1. Create a binary Tumor Mutation Burden (TMB) variable: TMB = 1 if a sample has ≥ 1 mutation, otherwise 0. Perform logistic regression of TMB on ancestry while controlling for age, gender, and subtype using the R formula: `TMB ~ ancestry + age + gender + subtype`.

steps.title: Apply FDR correction to regression p‑values
steps.instruction: Apply the Benjamini‑Hochberg false‑discovery‑rate (FDR) correction to all p‑values obtained from the logistic regression.

steps.title: Repeat analysis for EUR vs EAS ancestry
steps.instruction: Repeat steps 7–10, this time coding EUR as 0 and EAS as 1, to test somatic alterations between European and East Asian ancestries.

steps.title: Generate Q‑Q plot of associated genes
steps.instruction: Visualize the distribution of ancestry‑associated gene p‑values with a quantile‑quantile (Q‑Q) plot (see Figure 2A in Carrot‑Zhang et al., 2020).

steps.title: Perform cancer‑type‑specific analyses
steps.instruction: For each individual cancer type, repeat steps 7–9 (filtering, merging, regression) and generate Q‑Q plots, thereby obtaining cancer‑type‑specific ancestry‑association results.

steps.title: Validate genes using admixed individuals
steps.instruction: Using the previously excluded admixed samples (20 % < AFR ancestry < 80 %), calculate Spearman’s rank correlation between each gene’s mutation frequency and the individual’s fraction of AFR (or EAS) ancestry from ADMIXTURE. Test significance with a Wilcoxon rank‑sum test.

steps.title: Correlate mutational signatures with ancestry
steps.instruction: Download the mutational signature file (key resources). For each signature SBS1‑SBS50, fit a linear model controlling for age, gender, TMB, and subtype: `signature ~ ancestry + age + gender + subtype + TMB`.

steps.title: Apply FDR correction to signature p‑values
steps.instruction: Apply Benjamini‑Hochberg FDR correction to all p‑values obtained from the signature‑ancestry regressions.

steps.title: Correlate SCNAs, aneuploidy, and immune scores with ancestry
steps.instruction: Download TCGA arm‑level SCNA calls, genome‑doubling status, aneuploidy scores, and leukocyte fraction/immune infiltration scores (IMS). Perform logistic regression in Python with the formula: `ancestry ~ arm‑level SCNA + aneuploidy + genome_doubling + age + gender + subtype`.

steps.title: Apply FDR correction to SCNA p‑values
steps.instruction: Apply Benjamini‑Hochberg FDR correction to all p‑values from the SCNA/aneuploidy logistic regressions.

steps.title: Validate ancestry‑specific alterations in external cohort
steps.instruction: For genes with ancestry‑specific somatic alterations identified in cancer‑type‑specific analysis (FDR < 0.1), compare alteration frequencies between AFR vs EUR and EAS vs EUR using Fisher’s exact test in an independent cohort (e.g., Foundation Medicine). Ensure disease ontology terms are harmonized with TCGA and that ancestry calling follows the same pipeline.

steps.title: Power analysis for somatic mutation detection
steps.instruction: Simulate power to detect ancestry‑associated somatic mutations.

substeps.instruction: Read in TCGA ancestry assignments and cancer subtype annotations.
Assign a baseline mutation frequency (intercept) and an odds‑ratio (slope) for each simulated gene.
For each combination of frequency and odds‑ratio, run 1 000 generalized linear regressions of mutation status on ancestry (controlling for subtype).
Define power as the percentage of simulations with p‑value < 5e‑05 (Bonferroni‑adjusted threshold for ~20 000 genes).
Plot mutation frequency versus odds‑ratio with power curves.

steps.title: Power analysis for DNA methylation detection
steps.instruction: Simulate power to detect ancestry‑associated differential DNA methylation.

substeps.instruction: Simulate methylation levels for each HM450 CpG using a Beta(1,5) distribution for gender‑specific differences and a Normal(0.1,0.2) distribution (capped at 0 and 1) for subtype‑specific differences.
For each simulated methylation level, generate read counts as a Binomial(N = 40) variable, reflecting the average bead number per HM450 probe.
Repeat the simulation for all HM450 CpGs 1 000 times.
For each simulation, perform regression of methylation on ancestry while controlling for age, gender, subtype, and TMB.
Compute power as the fraction of simulations yielding significant ancestry‑specific methylation differences; plot power versus simulated methylation effect size.
Repeat the entire procedure for pan‑cancer and for each individual cancer type.
